nameStory: The Red-spotted Orbweaver gets its name from the distinctive reddish spots or markings that typically appear on its abdomen, making it stand out among its many orbweaver cousins. Like other orbweavers, it spins the classic circular webs we all recognize, with those perfectly spaced spiral threads radiating out from the center like spokes on a bicycle wheel.
description: The Red-spotted Orbweaver is a medium-sized spider that creates the classic round webs we often walk into on forest trails. Its most striking feature is the reddish spots or patches on its abdomen, which help distinguish it from other orbweavers in New England. These spiders typically have a rounded, somewhat flattened body shape and can vary in overall coloration from brownish to grayish, but those red markings are the key identifier.

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Look for distinctive reddish spots or patches on the abdomen - these may appear as bright red dots, streaks, or irregular patches that stand out against the spider's background color

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds classic orb webs with sticky spiral threads - the web feels distinctly sticky to the touch and has that perfect circular shape with radial support lines

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Has a rounded, somewhat flattened abdomen that's noticeably larger than the front body section (cephalothorax), giving it that classic orbweaver silhouette

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized for an orbweaver, with the body fitting comfortably on a dime or penny when legs are tucked in

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often sits in the center of its web during evening hours or hides at the web's edge during the day, connected by a signal thread that vibrates when prey is caught

habitat: Red-spotted Orbweavers prefer wooded areas and forest edges throughout New England, where they string their webs between shrubs, small trees, or tall vegetation. You're most likely to find them in mixed deciduous and coniferous forests, along woodland trails, or in areas where forest meets meadow. They seem to favor spots with some protection from wind but enough open space to build their circular webs.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin appearing as weather warms, with females starting to build their characteristic orb webs in protected woodland areas.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when webs are most visible and well-maintained, and you're most likely to spot the distinctive red markings as spiders are actively hunting.
seasonality.fall: Mating occurs and females may be seen with egg sacs; webs may become less perfect as spiders focus more on reproduction than web maintenance.
seasonality.winter: Adults typically die off after first hard frost, with eggs overwintering to hatch the following spring.

funFact: Despite being called 'red-spotted,' some individuals can have orange, pink, or even yellowish spots instead of true red - it's like they're wearing their own custom color scheme while keeping the same basic spotted pattern!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other Araneus orbweavers, especially the Marbled Orbweaver, but the red spotting pattern is distinctive. Memory trick: 'Red spots on the Orbweaver's rear' - the reddish markings are specifically on the abdomen, not the front body section.
compareHints: Among its Araneus relatives in New England, the Red-spotted Orbweaver is most easily distinguished by its reddish markings - the Cross Orbweaver has a white cross pattern, the Marbled Orbweaver has marbled yellow and brown coloring, and the Shamrock Orbweaver has a distinctive shamrock-like pattern. While several species can show reddish coloration, the specific spotted pattern of red markings on the abdomen sets this species apart from its cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its cousin the Marbled Orbweaver which has swirled, mottled patterns, the Cross Orbweaver's white cross marking is clean and distinct.

Among New England's Araneus orbweavers, the marbled orbweaver is unique for its extremely inflated, almost spherical abdomen—much rounder than the Cross Orbweaver's more egg-shaped belly or the Shamrock Orbweaver's triangular markings.

Among its Araneus cousins, the barn orbweaver is distinguished by its strong preference for wooden human structures, while the cross orbweaver favors gardens and the marbled orbweaver prefers trees and shrubs.

Among its Araneus cousins, the shamrock orbweaver's white spots make it relatively easy to distinguish - the cross orbweaver has a distinctive white cross pattern, while the marbled orbweaver shows complex marbled coloring without distinct dots.

Nordmann's Orbweaver is generally less distinctively marked than its famous cousins like the Cross Orbweaver (which has a prominent white cross pattern) or the Marbled Orbweaver (with its striking yellow and black marbled appearance).

Among the Araneus orbweavers, the Giant Lichen Orbweaver stands out for its specific lichen-mimicking camouflage, while relatives like the Cross Orbweaver have distinct white cross markings and the Marbled Orbweaver displays smooth, flowing color patterns.

Among its Araneus relatives, the Fierce Orbweaver stands out for its bold behavioral responses rather than distinctive markings like the Cross Orbweaver's white cross or the Marbled Orbweaver's marbled patterns.

Among its Araneus relatives, the Lattice Orbweaver's crosshatch pattern sets it apart from the distinctive white cross of the Cross Orbweaver and the swirled, marble-like patterns of the Marbled Orbweaver.
Unlike the Cross Orbweaver which prefers gardens and woodland edges, or the Marbled Orbweaver found on trees, the Openfield Orbweaver specifically chooses exposed grasslands and meadows.

Among the many Araneus orbweavers in New England, the Butterfly Orbweaver stands out for its wing-like geometric patterns rather than the cross-shaped markings of the Cross Orbweaver or the marble-stone appearance of the Marbled Orbweaver.
Among its many Araneus relatives in New England, the Juniper Orbweaver's defining characteristic is its habitat specialization rather than distinctive markings.

Unlike the Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross pattern on the back, or the Marbled Orbweaver with its orange and white marbled appearance, the White-bellied Orbweaver's key feature is underneath rather than on top.

Among its Araneus cousins in New England, the Red-backed Orbweaver's bright green front section makes it stand out from the typically brown or gray Cross Orbweaver and the yellow-and-black patterned Marbled Orbweaver.
Distinguishing Araneus iviei from its many orbweaver relatives in New England requires expert knowledge, as most species in this genus share similar web-building behavior and general body structure.

Unlike the common Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross marking, or the Marbled Orbweaver with its mottled, marbled pattern, the Black-spotted Orbweaver displays clear black spots as its defining feature.

Unlike the abundant Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross marking, or the variable Marbled Orbweaver with its yellow and black patterns, Araneus bonsallae lacks well-documented field marks for New England populations.

Unlike the common Cross Orbweaver with its white cross markings or the Marbled Orbweaver with its yellow and black patterns, the Humped bog orbweaver's most distinctive feature is its physical shape rather than its coloration.
